sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

Collecting research is the easy part. The hard part is making sense of it — turning scattered notes, summaries, and sources into a clear, organized understanding. This lesson covers AI-powered techniques for organizing what you've collected and synthesizing it into structured knowledge you can actually use.

## The Synthesis Problem

After researching a topic, most people have:
- Notes from multiple sources, often in different formats
- Bookmarks and links they haven't fully processed
- Partial summaries that don't connect to each other
- A general feeling of knowing more, but no clear structure

Synthesis means taking all of that and producing:
- A coherent mental model of the topic
- A structured document that captures what you've learned
- A clear view of what questions are answered and what remains open

AI is exceptionally good at this because it can hold large amounts of text in working memory and find patterns across it.

## Technique 1 — The Brain Dump Organiser

If you have scattered notes, don't try to organize them yourself first. Just paste everything into Claude and ask it to do the organizing:

```
Here are my research notes on [topic]. They're messy — different formats,
different sources, some overlap. Please:
1. Identify the main themes or categories across all these notes
2. Reorganize the content under those themes, keeping my original wording
3. Flag any contradictions between sources
4. List what seems to be missing based on the questions I haven't answered yet

[paste all your notes]
```

This typically turns 30 minutes of manual organizing into 60 seconds.

## Technique 2 — The Comparison Framework

When you have multiple sources saying different things, ask AI to create a structured comparison:

```
I have summaries from [X] sources on [topic]. Please create a comparison
table with these rows:
- Main argument or position
- Key evidence cited
- Assumptions made
- Limitations or caveats
- Date/source

[paste your summaries]
```

This works for comparing:
- Competitor products or services
- Different policy approaches
- Academic perspectives on a debate
- Industry analyst reports
- Job candidates (CVs)
- Vendor proposals

## Technique 3 — The Knowledge Map

For complex topics, ask AI to produce a structured map of the knowledge:

```
Based on my research notes below, create a knowledge map for [topic].
Structure it as:

## Core concepts (the things you must understand first)
## Key players or stakeholders
## Main debates or tensions
## What is well established
## What is contested or uncertain
## Open questions I still need to answer

[paste notes]
```

This gives you a structural overview you can use as a table of contents for a report, or as a framework for presenting findings.

## Technique 4 — The Gap Finder

AI can tell you what's missing from your research that you may not have thought to look for:

```
I've been researching [topic] for [purpose]. Here's what I've found so far:
[paste notes]

I need to produce [output: a report / presentation / recommendation].
What important aspects of this topic have I NOT covered yet?
What would a thorough researcher have looked into that I haven't?
What questions would my audience likely ask that I can't currently answer?
```

This is one of the most valuable prompts in the research workflow — it catches your blind spots before you commit to a final output.

## Building a Personal Knowledge Base

For ongoing research areas (topics you return to regularly), consider building a living knowledge base:

**Option 1 — Notion database:**
- Create a Notion database with columns: Topic, Source, Key Insight, Date, Reliability
- Use Notion AI to query across entries: *"What have I learned about X across all my entries?"*
- Each entry links to the source document

**Option 2 — Running document in Claude Projects:**
- Create a Claude Project (lesson 2-2)
- Upload your research files as project context
- Every conversation in that project has access to your knowledge base
- Claude answers questions using your specific documents

**Option 3 — NotebookLM notebook per topic:**
- Maintain a notebook per ongoing research area
- Add new documents as you find them
- The notebook grows as your research grows

The best option depends on how you work. Notion is best if you want structured entries with metadata. Claude Projects works well for document-heavy research. NotebookLM is best if your sources are primarily documents.

sections.title: Synthesize Your Research Notes
sections.content:
This workshop works best if you already have some research notes from lesson 15-2 or another recent research session. If not, spend 10 minutes collecting notes on any topic before starting.

**Step 1 — Gather your material**

Collect everything you have on a topic into one place:
- Notes from Perplexity searches
- Summaries from Claude conversations
- Key points you've copied from articles
- Your own observations or questions

It can be messy — that's fine. Paste it all into a document.

**Step 2 — Run the Brain Dump Organiser**

Open Claude.ai and paste everything with this prompt:
```
Here are my research notes on [topic]. They're unorganised. Please:
1. Group the content into 4-6 clear themes
2. Under each theme, list the key points in order of importance
3. Note any contradictions you find
4. List 5 questions I still haven't answered
```

**Step 3 — Run the Gap Finder**

Then ask:
```
I need to produce [your intended output] on this topic.
What important aspects have I not covered that I should research further?
```

**Step 4 — Build the structure**

Finally ask:
```
Based on everything I've shared, create an outline for a
[report / briefing / presentation] on this topic.
Use the themes you identified as main sections.
Under each section, note what content I already have and what I still need.
```

Save this outline. It becomes the template for your written output in lesson 15-6.

sections.question: You have 6 weeks of scattered research notes on a complex regulatory topic. You need to write a briefing paper by Friday. What is the most efficient first step?
options: Read all your notes from beginning to end to re-familiarise yourself
Start writing and see what you remember
Paste all your notes into Claude and ask it to identify themes, flag contradictions, and create an outline for the briefing
Search the topic fresh with Perplexity since your notes may be outdated
sections.explanation: Pasting all your notes into Claude to identify themes, contradictions, and produce an outline is the fastest path from scattered notes to a structured briefing. It takes seconds instead of the hour or more needed to manually re-read and reorganize. You'll then know exactly which sections need more research (the gap finder) and have a ready-made outline to write from. Re-reading (A) is slow. Starting blind (B) wastes time. Fresh search (C) may be part of filling gaps, but not before you know what gaps exist.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 15-5.** You now have four synthesis techniques — Brain Dump Organiser, Comparison Framework, Knowledge Map, and Gap Finder — and a clear path to building a personal knowledge base for ongoing research areas.
